title: From Ohio UFO Chase to Disclosure Day: Spielberg's Lifelong Alien Fascination
summary: In 1966, four police officers in Ohio chased a house-sized, egg-shaped UFO for nearly an hour across 70 miles. That real incident inspired an early sequence in Steven Spielberg's 1977 classic Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Now, nearly five decades later, Spielberg revisits the subject with Disclosure Day, in theaters as of June 12. The film imagines humanity receiving irrefutable proof of extraterrestrial life—and uncovering the powerful groups that kept it secret. Spielberg's connection to UFOs runs deep. Born in December 1946, he entered a world gripped by flying saucer fever; over 800 sightings were reported in his first year. Cold War nuclear fears fueled a collective anxiety that, as film historian Joseph McBride notes, found an outlet in UFO lore. But Spielberg's affinity for aliens also stems from personal history. His parents were children of Jewish immigrants, and more than a dozen relatives perished in the Holocaust. Growing up Jewish in increasingly WASPish communities heightened his sense of being an outsider. "Spielberg is always interested in the rewards and problems involved in the meeting of cultures," McBride tells Smithsonian. "UFOs and other forms of aliens fascinate him for that reason." As a teenager, Spielberg channeled this fascination into filmmaking, producing a $500 sci-fi thriller called Firelight at 17. After dropping out of college, he became the youngest director ever signed to a long-term studio contract. Disclosure Day screenwriter David Koepp calls the new movie "the summation of what he had to say on what is perhaps the single most important subject to him." It's a fitting capstone to a career populated with visitors from the stars.
why_it_matters: Spielberg’s lifelong fascination with aliens reflects humanity’s deep need to understand the unfamiliar, and ‘Disclosure Day’ arrives at a moment when real-world discussions about unidentified aerial phenomena and government transparency are more alive than ever—challenging young people to think about how we face evidence that could change our place in the cosmos.

keywords.explanation: Irrefutable means something that cannot be proved wrong or denied.
Extraterrestrial means coming from outside Earth; it is another word for alien.
Flying saucer fever describes a time when people were wildly excited and obsessed with reports of UFOs.
The Cold War was a long period of tension and threat of nuclear war between the United States and the Soviet Union after World War II.
The Holocaust was the genocide in which six million Jews were murdered by the Nazi regime during World War II.
WASPish describes communities or attitudes associated with White Anglo-Saxon Protestants, often the culturally dominant group in parts of America.

background_read: The modern UFO era began in 1947 when pilot Kenneth Arnold reported seeing nine saucer-like objects near Mount Rainier, and the term ‘flying saucer’ was born. That same summer, the Roswell incident in New Mexico—involving debris of a secret military balloon—sparked decades of conspiracy theories about government cover-ups of alien visitors.

Steven Spielberg’s Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977) arrived at the height of 1970s UFO fascination and stood out by portraying aliens not as invaders but as gentle, advanced beings seeking connection. The film deeply influenced pop culture and earned eight Academy Award nominations.

Spielberg’s own background is central to his storytelling: his father’s family fled persecution in Ukraine, and he grew up in suburban New Jersey and Arizona where he encountered anti-Semitic bullying. That feeling of being an outsider, alongside his parents’ divorce, fed themes of fractured families and longing for belonging that recur in his work.

The Cold War (1947–1991) between the U.S. and the Soviet Union created a constant dread of nuclear annihilation, and many historians note that UFO sightings often clustered around times of high international tension. Spielberg’s films repeatedly explore fear of the unknown, a sentiment that touched his own childhood during the Red Scare.

David Koepp, the screenwriter of Disclosure Day, previously collaborated with Spielberg on Jurassic Park (1993) and War of the Worlds (2005), making him a trusted partner in translating big, world-shaking ideas into intimate human stories.

perspectives.description: The film champions the idea that seeking truth, even uncomfortable truth, is a noble pursuit. For many, Spielberg’s optimistic take on aliens represents hope that contact with the ‘other’ can bring out the best in humanity rather than destroy it.

Critics argue that pouring resources and imagination into alien contact narratives can divert attention from urgent real-world crises like climate change or inequality. Some see the obsession with government UFO cover-ups as encouraging distrust without offering concrete solutions.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral – A product of its time and person
perspectives.description: The film is the natural endpoint of a career built on bridging the familiar and the strange. Spielberg’s outsider childhood and the Cold War backdrop are not just anecdotes—they are the DNA of a storytelling style that processes collective anxiety through safe, wondrous fiction.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking – What would real disclosure demand?
perspectives.description: ‘Disclosure Day’ could push a new generation to ask what society would actually do with irrefutable proof of extraterrestrial life. How would religions, governments, and everyday communities react? The movie might serve as a speculative laboratory for conversations we are only beginning to have.
